passage_text: Researchers at the University of Example investigated the impact of sleep deprivation on cognitive performance among college students. The study recruited 90 participants, randomly assigned to three groups: a control group that received a full 8 hours of sleep, a sleep‑deprivation group that slept only 4 hours, and a partial‑sleep group that slept 6 hours. Over a one‑week period, each participant completed a battery of reaction‑time tasks and accuracy tests. The results, summarized in Table 1, reveal that the control group exhibited the fastest average reaction time (420 ms) and highest accuracy (95 %). The sleep‑deprivation group had the slowest reaction time (480 ms) and lowest accuracy (85 %). The partial‑sleep group fell in between with a reaction time of 450 ms and accuracy of 90 %. These findings suggest that reduced sleep duration impairs both speed and precision of cognitive processing, supporting existing literature on the neurocognitive costs of sleep loss.
stem: Based on Table 1, which group exhibited the fastest average reaction time?

options.D: Control and partial‑sleep groups, which tied

explanation: Correct: The control group had the shortest reaction time, 420 ms, so it was fastest. Why the others are wrong: B) 480 ms is the slowest time, not the fastest. C) 450 ms is slower than 420 ms. D) The two groups differ (420 vs 450 ms), so there is no tie.
trap: Choosing the sleep-deprivation group by mixing up fastest with slowest, or by reading the larger number as better.

stem: Which experimental design best controls for confounding variables in this study?
explanation: Random assignment to groups in a randomized controlled trial minimizes confounding variables, ensuring that differences in outcomes are attributable to the intervention.
trap: Choosing an observational design because participants are followed for a week; only random assignment balances confounders between groups.

stem: What is the percent increase in reaction time of the sleep-deprivation group relative to the control group?
explanation: Percent increase = (480 – 420) / 420 × 100 = 14.3%, using the control as the reference value.
trap: 12.5% results from dividing by the sleep-deprivation value (480) instead of the control value (420).

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1?

options.A: Reaction time increased as sleep duration decreased.
options.B: Accuracy decreased as sleep duration decreased.
options.C: The 6-hour group fell between the 8-hour and 4-hour groups on both measures.
options.D: The 4-hour group had a faster mean reaction time than the control group.

explanation: Correct: The 4-hour group's mean reaction time was 480 ms, slower than the control's 420 ms, so D is not supported. Why the others are wrong: A) reaction times were 420, 450 and 480 ms for 8, 6 and 4 hours, so they rose as sleep fell. B) accuracy was 95, 90 and 85% for 8, 6 and 4 hours, so it fell as sleep fell. C) the 6-hour group had 450 ms and 90%, between the other two groups on both measures.
trap: Reading a larger reaction time as better performance and so reversing the direction of the effect.

stem: By how many percentage points did mean accuracy fall from the 8-hour control group to the 4-hour sleep-deprivation group?
explanation: Correct: Accuracy was 95% in the control group and 85% in the 4-hour group, a difference of 95 − 85 = 10 percentage points. Why the others are wrong: A) 5 points is the fall from 8 hours to 6 hours (95 to 90%). C) 15 points does not match any difference in the table. D) 60 is the reaction-time difference in milliseconds (480 − 420), a different variable.
trap: Using the 6-hour group or the reaction-time difference (60 ms) instead of the accuracy difference between the control and 4-hour groups.
